name: Birch sap

card.summary: A spring-tapped tree water used traditionally as a tonic and hair or freckle wash, now appearing in K-beauty serums; skin evidence is mostly lab-level.
card.note: Contact allergy to birch sap has been reported in case literature.

quick.overview:
Birch sap is a clear, slightly sweet liquid tapped from birch trees at the end of winter. It is drunk fresh or fermented in northern Europe and Asia and has folk uses for health, hair washing and fading freckles.

It appears as a hydrating ingredient in some skincare. The sources reviewed contain no human trials of its appearance effects; there is a 2024 laboratory-focused paper on skin whitening and an older report of contact allergy.
quick.mechanism: It is more than 99% water with small amounts of sugars, minerals such as manganese, amino acids and other plant compounds, which proponents cite for hydrating and antioxidant effects.
quick.risks: Birch pollen-allergic people may react; a 1980 report described immediate contact allergy to birch leaves and sap. Tapping can damage trees.

lead: Birch sap, also called birch water, is the liquid tapped from birch trees such as Betula pendula and B. pubescens during the spring thaw.[1] It is clear, slightly sweet and consumed fresh or fermented across boreal regions.[1]

Wikipedia records folk cosmetic uses in several countries, most commonly washing hair, and also against freckles, for hair growth and for skin lightening, and describes these as folk uses rather than established treatments.[1] In modern cosmetics it is used as a hydrating base ingredient.[2]
No human clinical trial of birch sap on appearance was found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Late winter to early spring, about a month
Over 99% water; sugars, manganese, amino acids

paras: Sap flows before leaf-out and turns bitter later in spring.[1] Per 100 g it provides about 4.6 kcal and about 1.1 g sugars, with manganese the most notable mineral.[1] Reported components also include amino acids, betulin and betulinic acid, and vitamins.[1] Fresh sap spoils quickly unless refrigerated, frozen or processed.[2]

Documented traditions include hair washing in Belarus, Estonia, Latvia and Poland, freckle treatment in the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary and Ukraine, hair growth in Bulgaria and baldness prevention in the United Kingdom.[1]

Folk medicine uses vary by region and include lung and kidney conditions, gout and jaundice.[1] Surveys of Russian medicinal plants for diabetes and of wild food use in Romanian regions list birch sap among traditional materials.[3][4] Grokipedia notes that high-quality evidence for major therapeutic benefits is limited.[2]

No studies found in humans for appearance outcomes. Related laboratory research includes a 2024 paper exploring white birch sap as an alternative to traditional skin-whitening agents,[5] whose full methods and findings were not reviewed here, and a 1980 report on immediate contact allergy to birch leaves and sap.[6]

The allergy report indicates birch sap can provoke immediate contact reactions in sensitised individuals.[6] Wikipedia notes birch tolerates tapping less well than maple and that tapping wounds often stain or decay, with no published evidence quantifying long-term tree effects.[1]
